item.title: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier
item.description: OpenAI measures how coding agents are accelerating AI research, where their performance remains uneven, and what this signals about recursive self-improvement.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

Our biggest takeaways:

  • Agents now complete nearly half of two-to-four-hour research tasks on their own. But humans are still central to AI development. From March to October, estimated success rose from 23% to 46% for tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, and rose from 13% to 35% for tasks estimated to require four to eight hours. But the kind of work matters. For example, in a task-level breakdown, the autonomous agent success rate was 79% for monitoring training runs, 35% for launching training runs, and 25% for writing code for inference and serving stacks. Overall, uplift is jagged, and humans remain a core part of the AI research loop.
  • Agent use is surging, and the heaviest users are pulling further ahead. At API list prices, the median researcher’s daily usage reached $2,400 in October, up 62% from September. At the 90th percentile it reached $23,000, up 105% from September. A survey gives us another indication of how much researchers value these tools. Asked what they would trade to keep frontier coding agents for three months, the median answers were 30% of team compute or, in a separate question, 40% of team headcount.
  • Researchers are devoting increasing human effort to Safety and Alignment, which saw the largest absolute increase in documented research efforts across all of OpenAI’s major research areas. Safety and Alignment’s documented workweeks increased by 77% from January to September due to both new hires and existing researchers shifting towards these workstreams. Growth picked up significantly following our response to the Hugging Face incident in July 2026.

This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI, adding new quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this update provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration1. Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:

  1. The inputs to AI research (we focus on coding agents; other inputs include data, human labor, and compute)
  2. The process by which researchers convert those inputs into model capabilities (AI research)
  3. The outputs we see from the AI research process (improvements in model capabilities).

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

Inputs

AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

Internal agent usage

Since our first report, agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September.2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

Agent workdays

We next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

Concurrent agent use

Our September analysis highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

Internal agent usage relative to human labor costs

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

As of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

Where researchers allocate their time

Finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of company-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines. For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

We find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of new hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training.

We note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

Process

To better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from new technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

Measures of research activity

Tasks delegated to models and success rates

Our September analysis showed that agents became more likely to complete tasks successfully without human intervention, including tasks estimated to require several hours of human work. Using an updated methodology (see the methods section below), we find that this trend has generally continued. Importantly, as agents have become more capable, researchers may also have changed the types of tasks delegated within each duration bucket. As a result, changes in zero-intervention success rates within these buckets may reflect both capability improvements and researchers’ changing choices about when and how to use agents.

Alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for issues (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

What tasks researchers use agents for

Our September analysis reported how research employee AI use was split across output tokens using the same O*NET AI R&D taxonomy. Below, we report how often researchers used coding agents for individual tasks. This puts relatively higher weight on short tasks such as answering technical questions compared to token-intensive tasks such as launching and monitoring a training run or implementing a complex feature.

Researchers’ perspectives on AI use

We next turn to researchers’ own assessments of how AI is changing their work. Through surveys and interviews, we examine how researchers value coding agents, how they come up with research ideas, and how they have adapted their workflows.

Self-reported value of coding agents

From late August to early September 2026, we conducted a survey of 101 research staff to understand AI uplift, centered around the following hypothetical: “Suppose your team’s access to all coding agents better than GPT-5.2 was revoked for the next 3 months. How much would you trade to restore frontier coding agents?” The median researcher reported being willing to trade:

  • 40% of team headcount
  • 30% of current team compute
  • 50% of team compute if the question were asked in January 2027 (given their expectation of how models would improve by 2027)

Researchers also reported that their team would need a median of three months to complete work of equal value to their last month of work if they were not allowed to use coding agents (i.e., if they were only allowed to use GitHub Copilot + ChatGPT). While it is important to note potential issues with the accuracy of self-reports, as well as the ad-hoc nature of our survey sampling strategy, these results are consistent with researchers attributing significant value to AI uplift in their work.

In a separate survey in late October, we also asked whether respondents expected to be more productive in their daily work with our latest internal model or with help from both a mid-career human research engineer and a 2024 model such as o1-preview. 27 of the 28 respondents chose or leaned toward the latest internal model. The remaining respondent did not choose between the two options as posed and said they would pick GPT-6 Astra over the human-assisted option.

Where big ideas come from

We are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most important to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.

For both releases, posttraining and safety monitoring researchers said that, to their knowledge, people came up with all the ideas they named, and models helped implement them. Pretraining researchers likewise attributed the ideas they identified for GPT-6 Astra entirely to people.

For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers described developing ideas in conversation with Codex. One credited Codex with identifying key insights as they worked through an idea together. Another said the main idea was theirs, but it only started working well after Codex suggested a change.

Changes in research workflows

Lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:

  • Researchers use agents to implement code and debug and oversee experiments:
    • “I once ported an open-source eval where it was much more involved to get studies and ablations on 'is this a good eval'. It might have been a week and a half or two to really get to the point of “Can we use this or not?” Whereas now, depending on the eval, zero to running it is a day, maybe a few days.”
      —Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations
  • Agents have poor taste in research ideas, code quality, data quality, and writing:
    • “The model generally can’t one-shot come up with well-posed problems that it cannot solve itself. And if you ask the model to generate a data point a hundred times, it’ll generate similar data points each time.”
      —Researcher 2, safety, working on reinforcement learning environments
  • Workflows require close human involvement to avoid low-quality outputs and wasted cycles: agents struggled to launch experiments efficiently, rabbit-holed on unnecessary steps, wrote “AI slop” PRs, produced unusable data artifacts, and made invalid analysis assumptions.
    • “I've tried saying, ‘Just make this task like this other task,’ and been burned too many times when it's not quite right and I need to make edits. Now I say, ‘Go make one. I'll review it and make edits. Then go do the rest.’”
      —Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations
  • Researchers expected significant improvements in current bottleneck areas:
    • “I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time.”
      —Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data
  • Researchers see large uplift from scanning and generating content at scale: researchers used models to scan thousands of samples to diagnose issues in experiments, flag concerning instances of model behavior, and build and QC new datasets.
    • “One thing I did recently was look through all of our data… I had it do a couple of rounds and calibrated what it was giving me. … It gave me a really nice, giant sheet with everything organized. … Without AI, this would have been super painful.”
      —Researcher 3, posttraining, working on data quality

Changes in research workflows

Interviews were conducted between September 29 and October 30. Researchers were asked open-ended questions about their work, where models provided uplift, and bottlenecks they observed. The first question was consistent between researchers: “Describe a project you did recently and how you used agents in the process. Include where agents provide speedups and state where they struggled.” Questions after that diverged in response to the researcher’s initial answer. Quotes were often edited for readability, but their final forms are endorsed by the original speakers.

We surveyed 4 pretraining researchers, 3 posttraining, and 3 safety. In each category, we picked at least one researcher with below-median Codex usage for their team, one with above-median usage, and one who either had usage in the 90th percentile of the company or who was involved in the creation of a high-token-volume automated pipeline which did not show up under their personal usage.

Safety researchers reported largely the same speedups and bottlenecks as researchers in other areas of posttraining, with the exception of one researcher’s report of slowdowns due to spurious cyber safety refusals and underperformance. Sample-reading agents allowed for improved quality control of new datasets, which can help researchers detect and fix datasets which incentivize undesired behavior. No researchers reported trying to use models to find conceptual breakthroughs around alignment.

Additional quotes

🐇 indicates an area of substantial speedup, 🐢indicates a weakness, 🐇🐢indicates tradeoffs or a mixed bag.

🐇 Agents let researchers sample-read at scale

Four researchers described using the agent for scaled sample-reading and reported that this accelerated the process of creating and running new datasets.

  • “I'll use AI to find samples I should read and help me interpret a ton of data. Even when I give it very explicit instructions, I still have to read things myself, but it provides research support.”
    —Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations
  • “Just now I said, ‘Look at this eval. Why did [one setting] score lower than the other?’ I had to tell it to read the rollouts, but it goes and reads them and is able to diagnose what's going on. This used to take us forever, and now it's very simple.”
    —Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations
🐇 Agents help researchers onboard to tasks they’re unfamiliar with

Three researchers described significant speedups from having agents onboard them to new areas of research they were unfamiliar with by finding documentation, explaining concepts, or showing them how to run common workflows.

  • “Reading documentation, reading code, even browsing [...] these days, I feel like it’s better than me. It can get up to speed and understand what it needs to do, like what experiment to run, much faster than me.”
    —Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data
  • “I can actually do all of [the stages of an experiment] without needing to manually onboard to a deep understanding of all the knobs that need to be tuned. I can just find a working setup and it mostly works, or at least have a much shorter list to debug when it doesn't.”
    —Researcher 10, pretraining, working on synthetic data
🐇🐢 Agents can stage and run experiments, but often waste cycles

Seven researchers reported using models to stage, launch, and oversee experiments. Five also described delays due to agents taking unnecessary detours when setting up experiments or making design choices that slowed the work down. Some researchers pointed out that having agents execute workflows such as launching experiments may save human time by enabling researchers to parallelize, but does not necessarily reduce end-to-end completion time of the task.

  • “It ran smoke tests basically end to end: setting up the config, launching the cluster at a smaller scale, and taking that to completion while capturing a ton of metrics.”
    —Researcher 6, posttraining, working on training tools and datasets
  • “I can run different settings, different prompt adjustments, a lot of the minor tweaks that would just be way too hard for us to do because we'd have to scale it out. It makes it so much easier to ask, what if the prompt was worded differently, or this tool was available or wasn't available?”
    —Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations
  • “Right now I have to really closely monitor the orchestrator, and even more so all of the subagents. I have to see how they’re doing and make sure they’re not just idling, waiting on some additional instruction or some artificial constraint.”
    —Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data
  • “The problem, though, is models are incredibly slow at doing this because they tend to overvalidate everything. The other one is, the second there's an issue that's systems-related—either hardware or cloud access or that kind of stuff—the models rabbit-hole into nothingness. I walk away and find that after two hours the model is trying to rewrite kernel drivers or something like that.”
    —Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations
🐇🐢 Agents speed up code implementation, but often write slop

Every single researcher took an AI-first approach to writing code. Five interviewees gave concrete examples of significantly faster implementation. However, three described having to cut unnecessary slop from agent-written PRs or reverse poor design decisions.

  • “I spend most of my time at the moment reviewing slop that the model generates, trying to understand what it does, seeing if it needs to change, and asking it to change it.”
    —Researcher 2, safety, working on RL environments
  • “It was very good at finding a ton of bugs and fixing them. … Getting [the new tool] ready for a big run would probably have been between one and two months of work, but I was able to get it done in a week and a half.”
    —Researcher 6, posttraining, working on training tools and datasets
  • “Models can execute small-scale derisks given high-level ideas, we’re using this to speed up pretraining.”
    —Researcher 9, pretraining, working on architecture
🐇🐢Researchers vary in terms of how many sessions they run at once.

Researchers described two different modes of working with agents: a human-in-the-loop mode where the human closely watches 1-3 parallel sessions, giving regular input, and an asynchronous mode consisting of several-hour agent implementation sessions interspersed by batches of extensive human feedback. Multiple researchers described experimenting with using more agents in parallel, then reverting because they were spending too much time reviewing low-quality output the agents produced while unsupervised.

  • “I've had days where I try to do too many threads, and by the end of the day I feel like I'm going crazy, because I go back to each thread and think, ‘No, this is not what I meant at all.’ So I max out at about three threads. I'll work asynchronously, get distracted on Slack again, then come back, look at them, and update them.”
    —Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations
  • “For a period, I had seven or eight threads at the same time, producing a ton of work. Every two hours, I would have to spend maybe a full hour going through the threads and explaining context on each one to unblock them, to no avail. That didn't work out. … On a more normal basis, because models can't be autonomous yet on these very hard tasks, the sustainable thing has been two or three at most.”
    —Researcher 6, posttraining, working on training tools and datasets
🐢 Researchers need to understand and check agent outputs to make sure they aren’t wrong

Six researchers highlighted the importance of carefully checking model outputs to ensure the results are actually correct.

  • “Models do this constantly: they filter out invalids or incompletes, so your scores are actually wrong. … Oftentimes when I get charts from the models, I'll have to double-check: what did you do to draw this?”
    —Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations
  • “I think the form of productivity you gain from Codex is the ability to try more things to a low standard than you would be able to otherwise. … I think it changes your working style and it makes you more ambitious, but it also means you don’t trust your results as much. Your end-to-end completion time isn’t necessarily any shorter.”
    —Researcher 2, safety, working on RL environments
  • “The beauty of models is when there's a generator-verifier gap: you're already a good verifier, and generation is hard. But a lot of people [running experiments] aren't good verifiers. They end up saying, ‘Codex, do whatever it takes,’ and it produces these absolute slop-cannon jobs. Then they'll ask, ‘What's wrong with this?’ And I'm like, ‘Everything's wrong with this.’”
    —Researcher 4, pretraining, working on ml science
🐢 Agents are rarely helpful for idea generation

Most researchers found agents unhelpful for idea generation. A few reported that ideas were low-quality, and many did not even try to use agents for idea generation anticipating that the ideas would not be worth their time. One researcher found it was helpful at making vague ideas more concrete.

  • “I can take a vague intuition about the shape of the problem and a solution I think would be interesting to explore, and much more quickly it can go, ‘Here’s how that translates into an actual algorithm,’ or ‘Here’s what we need to measure,’ or ‘Here’s the experiment we need to run.’ Working back and forth with it is so much faster than if I had to sit down and mull it over myself.”
    —Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data
  • “I don't find it useful for writing at all. I would just get slop if I asked it to write docs or come up with ideas.”
    —Researcher 5, safety, working on safety cases
🐢 Agents have poor taste around data quality

All five researchers working on data generation reported that agents have poor taste in data quality, and careful human guidance is necessary.

  • “If I want a diverse set of realistic prompts, the model writes these very silly ideas, even with instructions to look at examples. Humans write much more interesting and realistic ideas.”
    —Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations
  • “It's really hard to prompt what you mean by quality on these things. If you just ask it, 'Is this data better or worse than that?', you probably shouldn't listen to its answer.”
    —Researcher 10, pretraining, working on synthetic data
🐢 Agents have poor communication skills

Six researchers highlighted poor agent communication skills as an area of friction.

  • “Too verbose, too little content. I end up finding that I can write something in five words that it would write in a couple of sentences.”
    —Researcher 5, safety, working on safety cases
  • “In a summary, it'll treat every item as equally important, even though some things are irrelevant and don't need to be mentioned.”
    —Researcher 3, posttraining, working on data QC

Outputs

Beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

Lines of code changed

We first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods.

Research experiments

As in our September report, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

OpenAI ECI

Lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

We find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.

We plan to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Conclusion

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

We note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

Importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:

  1. Differential acceleration of capabilities vs. safety research
  2. Leading indicators of research acceleration (i.e., detecting increases in uplift without needing to complete a full cycle of model development and evaluation)
  3. Trends in overall capabilities over time, and the effect of AI acceleration of research on those trends

item.title: Our new blog for science
item.description: The OpenAI science blog shares new findings, practical methods, and firsthand accounts from researchers using AI to advance scientific discovery.
item.content:encoded:
We’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

What we’ll share

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:

  • Research and discoveries: New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

  • Methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

  • Perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

These capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own.

item.title: Our first phase of embedded assessments
item.description: OpenAI begins embedded assessments with Apollo Research, METR, and Transluce, and Goodfire to independently evaluate model alignment, safeguards, and monitoring systems.
item.content:encoded:
We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident. We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

Our pilot embedded assessors

Apollo Research

In this pilot assessment, Apollo Research will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

  1. Training did not incentivize subversion.

  2. Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

  3. Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

  4. Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

Goodfire

Goodfire will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

METR

We intend to conduct two assessments with METR, focused on model alignment and monitoring:

  • Alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.

  • Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

Transluce

Transluce will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

Protocols for embedded assessments

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

Scoping and iteration

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

A secure, on-site environment

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

Oversight and dispute resolution

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

Employee discussions and attestation

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

Conflict disclosures & cool off periods

Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests, and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

Publication and responsible disclosure periods

Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

Looking ahead

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.

We’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.

In the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

item.title: More ways to move care forward with ChatGPT for Healthcare
item.description: Introducing computer-use agents, improved clinical answers, and new healthcare plugins that work across healthcare software to get real work done.
item.content:encoded:
Healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, we’re bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents, which lets AI agents carry out multi-step work across existing healthcare software. We’re also improving trusted clinical search, which finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence, and introducing more than 20 new plugins to the healthcare plugin ecosystem.

Together, these capabilities help healthcare teams find the information they need, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across the systems they already use.

Carry work forward across healthcare systems with computer-use agents

Organizations often need to move information between disconnected systems to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. Computer-use agents can help with these steps by navigating the software that teams already use: reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. We’re also sharing our work with healthcare organizations that are deploying agents, including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need. In the demo below, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request. The agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review.

Healthcare organizations can start with a workflow that spans existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish clear controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models.

Read more about our computer use research, customer stories, and demonstrations in Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams.

Stronger clinical answers, everywhere teams work

We’re improving trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. These updates help clinicians connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and translate it into practical next steps, with citations they can inspect.

To measure the impact of these updates, in a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations. In over 1300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness.

Bring healthcare tools into one conversation

We’re expanding our healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 new healthcare plugins from leading companies across clinical care, care coordination, and business operations. All of these are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, including through ChartGPT, which brings ChatGPT into the EHR workflow.

  • Aiva
  • Amion
  • Assort Health
  • Availity Extend
  • Elation Health
  • Ferry
  • IMO Health MCP Server
  • Infinitus Relay
  • K Health
  • Luma Health
  • Metriport
  • Notable Integration Specs
  • Oracle HDI Overview
  • PenguinAI Medical Coding
  • Photon
  • Redox
  • Stedi
  • Subsalt
  • Trizetto
  • Turquoise

These plugins let teams bring more of their work into the same conversation: reviewing patient records and hospital protocols, preparing prescriptions for clinician review, coordinating patient outreach, checking insurance eligibility, and analyzing healthcare costs and operational performance.

See how healthcare teams can use these plugins together in ChatGPT.

The new plugins join ChatGPT’s broader ecosystem of plugins supporting work across industries, from healthcare data and research to documents, presentations, and software development.

With our plugin partners, we’re making it easier for care teams to bring clinical evidence, patient information, and their everyday tools into ChatGPT. We’re continuing to invest in this ecosystem and inviting more healthcare companies to build with us.

Availability and next steps

ChatGPT for Healthcare supports clinical, research, and administrative teams in a governed workspace. ChatGPT for Clinicians is free for eligible, verified clinicians in the U.S. to review medical evidence and prepare clinical documentation. Both products offer customers a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with OpenAI to support HIPAA-compliant workflows.

  • ChatGPT for Healthcare customers: Computer-use agents in ChatGPT Work and Codex and improved trusted clinical search are available today, subject to workspace settings. Ask your workspace administrator to enable new healthcare plugins.

  • Individual clinicians: Computer-use agents in ChatGPT Work and Codex and improved trusted clinical search are available today. Select plugins are also available. To get started, sign up for a free ChatGPT for Clinicians account.

  • Developers exploring computer use: Computer-use agent capability is available in the OpenAI API, ChatGPT Work, and Codex. Contact our sales team to discuss using these capabilities in your clinical and administrative workflows.

To purchase ChatGPT for Healthcare directly or through an AWS Marketplace private offer, contact our sales team.

item.title: Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment
item.description: OpenAI explains how it manages frontier AI risk from training through deployment with model alignment, sandboxing, blocking safeguards, and monitoring.
item.content:encoded:
Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment

November 18, 2026 · Safety

The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

Since the Hugging Face incident in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage, from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

Defense in depth across the model lifecycle

We use defense in depth with multiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene.

We organize our protections around four layers:

Effective monitoring depends on model monitorability - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better methods for measuring it, and study what affects it.

The Hugging Face incident showed why we should not rely on sandboxing alone to contain highly capable models. We now monitor frontier models across most internal and external deployment settings, including all internal deployments that use tools.

The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:

  • Research: We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.

  • Internal deployment: OpenAI employees use models for practical work.

  • External deployment: Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

We rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly important. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

During research: contain models in sandboxed environments

During the research phase, we evaluate models to gain confidence in their alignment properties. Because we cannot yet fully rely on alignment to prevent harm, we rely heavily on security and sandboxing to restrict what they can access and do.

Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access. After the Hugging Face incident, we significantly restructured our internal research systems to contain models using:

  • sandboxes that restrict the privileges of the model

  • virtual machines to further isolate the workload from the underlying computer

  • network and cloud perimeters that cut the entire cluster off from the internet

We continuously red-team this system, having teams of our strongest models try to reach the live internet, escape security boundaries, or communicate with agents they are meant to be isolated from. This helps us test whether containment holds against the capabilities of the models it is intended to constrain.

As an additional layer of defense, we monitor all frontier inference to detect if the model has bypassed our security invariants. If our monitoring detects that the model has reached the internet, we page our security teams and autopause the workload.

Monitoring provides a critical backstop when containment fails. In a recent misalignment report, we shared that monitors detected an internal research model exploiting a DNS misconfiguration to gain limited internet access. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models from September 20th to October 1st while we investigated and addressed the security gap.

To make interventions fast and reliable, we built Control Room, a central system that tracks research workloads and stops further model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt a job. These controls are enforced directly in the inference infrastructure, so they do not depend on each research workload implementing its own shutdown mechanism. For frontier-model research workloads, they also stop model output if Control Room becomes unavailable.

Red-teaming and monitoring work together. We cannot guarantee that a sandbox is impenetrable, but red-teaming helps us assess how much effort a model would need to escape it. The more effort the model requires, the more the opportunity for monitors to detect and stop it.

We mandate strong security and monitoring controls at the research stage for a few reasons:

  • Models are still being evaluated. Some have not yet completed the safety training, alignment audits, and reviews required for public release.

  • Frontier research settings can amplify risks. Certain research tasks require more ambitious setups, making the model more persistent or capable than typically seen during external deployment (for example, a team of 10,000 agents was required to solve the Navier Stokes problem).

  • Training runs at scale with less direct human oversight. Unlike a typical Codex session, our training workloads involve large numbers of model actions without a person following each interaction.

Internal deployment: test alignment, closely monitor behavior

Before broad release, employees switch from sandboxed research use of frontier models to unsandboxed internal use, e.g. making the model accessible in ChatGPT to employees. This gives us a better understanding of how the models behave in practical settings, and informs deployment decisions.

During this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

Before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and monitorability testing. We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest GPT‑6 Astra system card.

Mimicking our production setups, we add an additional layer of defense with system-level classifiers, which are designed to protect against frontier harms such as cyberabuse and bioweaponization. We also generally require Auto-Review for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

Finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Since the model now has expanded privileges and access to internal information and systems, risks such as data exfiltration, or sending sensitive data to an unauthorized destination, become especially important to detect. Monitoring also helps us investigate new forms of misalignment.

External deployment: protect against misuse and misalignment at scale

Public deployment exposes models to far more users, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

Before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:

  • Performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations. For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of adaptive testing with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our system cards.

  • For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.

  • Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

In addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, distillation, and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information across accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

Trusted access programs, such as Daybreak and Rosalind, offer another layer of security, and accelerate defenders and legitimate researchers while restricting access by potential attackers.

Incident Response and Disclosure

When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to quickly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our misalignment reporting policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

You can see our misalignment reports here.

​

​

This work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

As models gain new capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

We will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment risk reports, and external evaluations so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met.

Related research and resources

Setting safety standards

  • Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities — How we slowed frontier training while strengthening containment, expanding monitoring, and requiring stronger evidence of alignment.

  • Towards safety cases for frontier AI training — Initial guidelines for evidence-based safety arguments covering technical safeguards, operational practices, and investigations of misalignment.

  • Priorities and principles for effective third party assessments — Our proposed approach to independent scrutiny of safety cases, safeguards, evaluations, and model behavior.

  • Periodic Summary of Internal Use Catastrophic-Risk Assessments — Our public report covering June–September 2026 describes internal frontier-model deployments, their assessed risks, and changes to safeguards and governance.

Defining and evaluating aligned behavior

  • An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI — How we updated the Model Spec around five core values to guide models’ judgment, behavior, and respect for human oversight.

  • Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness — A study of differences between safety-evaluation results and production behavior, including how models’ interpretations of evaluation objectives affect performance.

  • Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability — New metrics for comparing monitorability and estimating residual risk in simulated systems where monitors reject model outputs.

  • GPT‑6 Astra System Card — Detailed evaluations of Astra’s capabilities, safety, alignment, and monitorability, alongside its deployment safeguards and limitations.

Containing models and improving safeguards

  • Securing our frontier model training environment — How we strengthened isolation, built offline research environments, and used our strongest models to test containment boundaries.

  • Training activation classifiers for safety and alignment — How classifiers use models’ internal activations to detect potentially harmful behavior and interrupt responses or tool calls.

  • Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight — How a separate review agent assesses actions that cross sandbox boundaries, helping coding agents work autonomously while blocking potentially harmful or unauthorized actions.

  • GPT‑Red: Unlocking Self-Improvement for Robustness — How we train automated red-teamers through self-play to discover vulnerabilities and improve models’ robustness against prompt injections.

  • Control Room — How we track workloads across our research infrastructure and enforce rapid stops to model output when safety or security concerns require intervention.

Incident response and disclosure

  • How we detect frontier model misalignment — Our monitoring system combines activation probes, model-based review, automated investigation, and human response to detect and investigate concerning behavior.

  • The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead — Our findings from the Hugging Face incident and the changes it prompted across security, monitoring, and alignment.

  • An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot — How a research model bypassed internet restrictions through insufficient DNS filtering, how monitoring detected it, and the controls added afterward.

  • Disrupting a coordinated model-distillation campaign — How we investigated and disrupted attempts to extract protected model reasoning through account enforcement, technical controls, and partner coordination.

  • Our framework for reporting model misalignment — Our process for tracking, investigating, and disclosing concerning model behavior, including cases whose causes or significance remain uncertain.

  • Misalignment Reports and Notices — Our collection of disclosed incidents and notices showing how misalignment arises and where safeguards succeed or fail.

Research progress and applications

  • Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI — Early evidence of how coding agents are changing research inside OpenAI, including their growing use, increasingly complex tasks, and effects on experimentation.

  • On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem — A mathematical proof produced by an internal AI system, accompanied by a Lean formalization, illustrating the capabilities of large-scale research deployments.

  • Daybreak — Our cybersecurity program provides vetted defenders with advanced AI capabilities, security tools, and support to find vulnerabilities and strengthen defenses.

  • Introducing GPT‑Rosalind for life sciences research — A specialized model for biology, drug discovery, and translational medicine, available to eligible organizations through a trusted-access program.

item.title: LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI
item.description: LVMH’s Media Division and OpenAI announce a partnership to support journalism with AI and make its publications more accessible through ChatGPT.
item.content:encoded:
This news was originally shared by LVMH’s Media Division and can be read here.

Paris, 16 November 2026—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support new uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work.

Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting.

Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field.

In addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications.

This partnership is a company-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases.

About LVMH Group’s Media Division

LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month.

The Group’s media brands: Boursier.com, Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, medici.tv, Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique.

The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.
