item.title: Introducing OpenAI for Chile
item.description: OpenAI and the Government of Chile are partnering to support responsible AI adoption, build public-sector skills and help local startups develop AI applications.
item.content:encoded:
Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.

The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action plan, which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile.

The partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program, of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

Putting AI to work in Chile

The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting new models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel.

For civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.

To support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities.

A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

Specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use.

About OpenAI for Countries

OpenAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

item.title: Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol
item.description: Introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, with better professional outputs, coding, computer use, and efficiency at lower cost across ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API.
item.content:encoded:
A new standard for professional work

Try in ChatGPT Work

We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works.

In the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task.

GPT-6.2 Sol: our go-to model for everyday work

Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid plan. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks.

In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

Its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the important tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released LifeVal evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost.

Professional outputs that match industry standards

We trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler.

Harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. Astra for Law, our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark.

Our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of GDPval that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. GPT‑6.2 Astra leads the models we tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT‑6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens. GPT‑6.2 Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT‑6.1 Sol.

Building a valuation workbook or writing an investment memo starts with finding the relevant figures in source files and working out how they fit together. Artificial Analysis’s AA‑AnalystAgent tests that work on real spreadsheets and reports. In one task, models use California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate how much the program spent on medical transport. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, answering 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts.

GPT‑6.2 Astra is our best model yet at designing slides and following slide templates, whether given an original file or even a screenshot. It can match the layout, colors, and typography down to the exact font size, and carry the template’s writing style into new slides. Early testers found the decks easier to use directly with fewer edits, thanks to titles that state the main takeaway and concise body copy that focuses on the details readers need.

Computer use and interactive web design

GPT‑6.2 Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. Engineers can use that additional detail to check how components fit, see where loads shift as a design moves, and test revisions before building a prototype.

We asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road. Astra created the 3D model and wrote a Python solver to simulate complex dynamics between the tires and suspension, then animated the results in Blender. This enables engineers to quickly test new designs and improve simulation accuracy over time.

GPT‑6.2 Astra can model a mechanical system part by part, giving engineers a way to show how it goes together and test how design changes affect its behavior.

Our team used GPT‑6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a lamp. The video follows the design from reference photos through CAD revisions to a physical lamp assembled by hand. The site, generated by GPT-6.2 Astra, can be used to create your own paper lamp.

GPT‑6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look and building elements around the actual goal of the site.

Those gains in visual reasoning and computer use carry over to 3D design. GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, from a pinball table you can play to a recreation of the Colosseum you can explore from different angles. On Artificial Analysis’s AA‑3D, human judges try two blinded experiences built from the same prompt and vote for the one they prefer. GPT‑6.2 Astra ranks first with 1,318 Elo, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT‑6.2 Sol at 1,259.

Efficient workflows with cleaner code style

GPT‑6.2 Astra has better judgment about how to execute a task, including matching its tools and effort to the workflow, and knowing when to use plugins versus computer use.

On coding, GPT-6.2 Astra is better at implementing and testing complex changes in existing codebases. Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision.

Cybersecurity capabilities

GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol mark another significant jump in cyber capabilities. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations. Like GPT‑6 Astra, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework.

Due to their increased capabilities, we’re launching GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance. These protections reduce misuse risk, but also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows. Through OpenAI Daybreak, defenders can currently access GPT‑6 Sol with reduced cyber refusals on Daybreak Blue, in addition to our alpha for GPT-6 Astra, and GPT‑6 Cyber for advanced, authorized security testing on Daybreak Red. We will work to bring GPT‑6.2 models to Daybreak.

We highlight key benchmark results below, using internal testing configurations with cybersecurity safeguards and classifiers disabled. See the accompanying system card for full results and methodology.

Developers increasingly rely on coding agents to write production software, even as more capable agents lower the barrier to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. PHP2Shell showed how AI can help researchers uncover critical flaws. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, we made defensive capabilities a core focus, introducing new training signals to help developers prevent and repair those flaws—writing secure code from the start and producing patches that preserve intended behavior.

Safety and alignment

We're deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with our strongest safeguards to date. We've tightened restrictions and strengthened the systems we use to monitor models and intervene when needed.

Like GPT-6 Astra, in addition to meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity, both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet the High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under our Preparedness Framework. We’ve implemented protections to mitigate the associated risks, alongside increased restrictions across a set of potential dual-use biological and cybersecurity requests.

More details about our safeguards and testing are available in the GPT-6.2 system card.

GPT-6.2 Astra is our first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI Self-improvement, which measures a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. A ‘High’ designation reflects our assessment that the model’s impact is equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher an additional, highly capable research engineer as an assistant, relative to their 2024 baseline. We track this capability because models that can help develop future AI systems could also introduce new risks to safety, like accelerating progress faster than safeguards or human oversight can adapt.

To address these risks, we’ve built more oversight and controls into how we train and deploy our models. Before expanding internal access to GPT-6.2 Astra, we evaluated its alignment and verified that required safeguards were in place at each stage. We strengthened containment in our research environments, and tested those protections with our most capable models. We also built Control Room, a system that tracks research workloads and can halt further model output when intervention is needed. Our expanded monitoring examines models’ reasoning and actions across internal workloads and supported external deployments. It can automatically flag unauthorized behavior, and, where supported, pause workloads or conversations.

Both models performed similarly to GPT-6 Astra on most alignment evaluations, and took fewer improper actions in simulated workplace tasks. However, in two tests, they were more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file or unavailable search tool. We added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce these omissions, and we’re continuing to investigate the behavior.

Pricing and availability

Starting today, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pro 500 subscribers can use Ultrafast with either model. For the first time, we’re also bringing Ultrafast to Pro 200 subscribers, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol. Eligible Enterprise and Edu users get the same access once their workspace admin enables it. Developers can also access gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol through the OpenAI API, with Ultrafast available for both models at launch.

GPT‑6.2 Astra costs significantly less per task than GPT‑6 Astra, driven by better token efficiency, a 20% discount on input and output tokens, and a deeper 60% discount on cached input tokens. Standard API rates per million tokens are $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. GPT‑6.2 Sol carries forward GPT‑6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output per million tokens.

For GPT-6.2 Astra & Sol, in order to improve cache reuse, help lower costs and latency, and preserve reasoning across turns, we recommend keeping prompt prefixes unchanged and appending new instructions to the conversation.

item.title: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet
item.description: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet, a secure way for agents in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots to complete purchases with user approval and existing card protections.
item.content:encoded:
We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents. It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes. Built in partnership with American Express, Chase, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available through dots for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US. Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re releasing tools and guidance to help businesses support customers using agents.

1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems.

To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.

How a purchase works

ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. Users add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service.

Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization.

Equipping businesses for agentic commerce

Agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition.

Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing a Commerce Partner Playbook with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers:

  • Help customers find accurate product information. Claim your business in ChatGPT and, once verified, update your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability.

  • Ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website. Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed.

  • Work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases. Wallet’s payment tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations. You can work with your providers to understand how they recognize these transactions. We’re also working with fraud prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and payment service providers including Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe to help their systems recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.

  • Give agents more ways to work with your business. Build a plugin to let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions through your existing systems. Websites can also add WebMCP tools.

Availability

ChatGPT Wallet begins rolling out today in dots, enabling users to have their dot complete purchases on their behalf. It will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US with eligible US-issued cards. We’ll work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to learn from early use and expand availability, helping more customers and businesses benefit from agentic commerce.

item.title: Introducing ChatGPT for Sales

A starting point for every seller

The new Sales plugin from OpenAI gives you ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up. Sales teams work best when everyone has a shared understanding of the customer. Which accounts are worth pursuing? What does a buyer need to move forward? Which deals need attention, and why? The answers often sit across teammates, prospecting tools, customer calls, and the CRM. Bringing that information together gives teams more time to make informed decisions and follow through on customer commitments. That starts with the work you do every day.

Connect your sales process to ChatGPT

ChatGPT for Sales brings your tools, customer context, and sales workflows into one place. It also gives your team access to partner plugins, so ChatGPT can use customer context from your existing tools to help move opportunities forward. Choose the partner plugins that fit your sales process.

Build tailored presentations with ChatGPT Slides, Gamma, Figma, or Canva, or create an interactive demo or ROI calculator with ChatGPT Sites.

Use cases for every sales team

Build pipeline in the right accounts

Make a stronger case to each buyer

Keep deals moving with clear next steps

See where your pipeline is at risk

How sales teams are winning with ChatGPT

Get started

ChatGPT Business and Enterprise admins can enable ChatGPT for Sales for your team by opening the Admin Console, selecting your workspace, and selecting Plugins. Make the Sales plugin and relevant partner plugins available for members to install, or install them by default for your team. Review access to the required apps and the actions they can use. Workspace members can complete any required account connections when prompted.

We’re continuing to build ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugin ecosystem around the work sales teams do every day. Our goal is to bring more of that work into ChatGPT, with connected tools and customer context that carries from finding an opportunity to preparing for a conversation and following through.

item.title: Inside the Codex sandbox
item.description: See how Codex runs commands on your machine while enforcing the filesystem and network limits you control across macOS, Linux, and Windows.

At OpenAI, we take a defense in depth approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex, to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

A sandbox limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users configure the Codex sandbox through permission profiles, which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

In this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end users and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

Choosing the sandbox boundaries

In Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile:

  • Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks.

  • Allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys).

  • Disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read. It also prevents legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies, which require additional access.

These restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior, but harmful actions are still possible. For example, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier. Such a change might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git. If the user’s editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox. This is why we take a defense in depth approach: the sandbox limits what commands can access, while training and alignment help the model use that access in accordance with the user’s intent.

For guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment, see the Codex security cookbook.

Designing the sandbox

Virtual machines and containers are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.

For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

For example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

The harness exposes these OS-specific sandboxing mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. This API takes a command and a permission profile. If the permission profile allows limited network access, the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits:

Python

This function starts the process in a sandbox and returns a Child handle the harness can use to wait for it to finish. Each child process inherits its parent’s sandbox constraints, so those restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together, from configuration to running a sandboxed command. The sections that follow explain each stage.

How the harness leverages the sandbox

As explained in Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop, the Codex harness is responsible for executing tool calls generated by the model. For coding tasks, the most commonly used tool is a shell tool, which runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. Here we’ll examine the one-shot exec_command shell tool to illustrate how the harness employs the sandbox to achieve the desired protections.

This is a simplified version of how the exec_command tool call would be honored by the Codex harness without sandboxing:

Python

To sandbox the command, the harness replaces the call to subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(). The harness supplies the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy:

Python

The exec_command tool also lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, but the harness decides whether to grant the request:

Python

When use_default is specified, the harness uses the default sandbox config for the turn. with_additional_permissions requests expanded access within the sandbox, while require_escalated requests execution outside it. The harness evaluates the request based on the user’s preferences before executing the command. (For example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review.) If execution is authorized, Codex will pass the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy to perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing() with the command arguments from the original ExecCommandToolCall.

The shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files. This reuse extends beyond the harness: the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools, as we’ll see later. Next, we’ll look at how permission profiles are defined.

Configuring the sandbox

A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects. You can define your own profiles under [permissions] in config.toml. For example, the following defines a profile named dev that extends the built-in :workspace profile:

TOML

The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace. Filesystem entries can grant read-only access (read), grant read and write access (write), or block access entirely (deny).

The :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project’s workspace roots. By default, the Codex CLI uses its working directory as its sole workspace root, while the ChatGPT desktop app uses the project’s source folders. Codex applies each rule to every root, so the .vscode entry in dev makes the .vscode directory read-only under each root.

In addition to its own rules, dev inherits the following protections from :workspace:

TOML

Network permissions

When it comes to configuring the network for the sandbox in Codex, there are roughly three options:

  • Disable all network access (default for the :workspace profile)

  • Enable full, direct network access (default for the :danger-full-access profile)

  • Restrict network access to a proxy, which decides what to let through based on the permission profile


To give dev direct network access, set permissions.dev.network.enabled = true at the top level of config.toml. This grants full network access when the network proxy is disabled.

To restrict dev to a set of domains, enable the network proxy and configure its domain rules:

TOML

Domain rules support exact names and wildcard patterns, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules. Requests to other domains require approval or are blocked, as described in Network proxy below.

Layering configuration and enforcing limits

Individual users can configure defaults that apply across projects and override them for a particular trusted project. Enterprise administrators may also want to configure defaults for their users and constrain which settings those users can change. Codex supports both through layered configuration and managed requirements.

As described in Configuration precedence, Codex merges settings from multiple config.toml files. Tables are merged recursively, with the higher-precedence source winning when values conflict. Arrays are replaced as a whole.

This is why permission profiles use tables for filesystem paths and network domains. A team can add or override individual entries in its own configuration and automatically inherit changes to all other entries in the organization’s base configuration:

TOML

Administrators can also supply managed requirements through requirements.toml to constrain users’ configuration choices. These requirements can come from multiple sources, including system files and cloud-provided policy. A common use case is to specify allowed_permission_profiles to constrain the set of permission profiles an enterprise user can select. For example, an administrator could specify these cloud requirements:

TOML

The cloud requirements would take precedence over the system requirements file at /etc/codex/requirements.toml, so an entry in that file cannot override the explicit ":danger-full-access" = false above. Leaving :workspace unspecified allows another requirements layer to supply that entry. Profiles whose entries are false or absent from the final merged table are unavailable.

This separation lets organizations enforce limits while users tailor their configuration within those limits. The resulting permission profiles can be used by the harness or applied directly to a command, as we’ll see next.

Using the codex sandbox command

The Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config. This is commonly used to test out the profile, ensuring that the sandbox prevents the behavior it was designed to block.

For example, the following command attempts to configure VS Code to run a malicious auto-formatter on save. Assuming .vscode already exists, the dev profile defined above should block this write because that directory is read-only (codex sandbox treats cwd as a workspace root by default):

Bash

Indeed, on macOS this fails with:

Plain text

The codex sandbox command makes Codex’s sandboxing mechanism available independently of an agent session. You can use the same configuration language and platform-specific enforcement to constrain commands launched by your own tools.

Example: sandboxing an MCP server

For a stdio MCP server configured in config.toml, the Codex harness does not attempt to sandbox the command used to start the server. Codex cannot reliably infer which files or network services that server needs, so applying a default sandbox profile could break an otherwise valid configuration.

For example, the standard way to configure the @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory MCP server for use with Codex is as follows:

TOML

Because this npx command runs unsandboxed, it can write files and make network requests with the same permissions as the user running Codex, which is overly permissive. To lock it down, we can define a permission profile named memory-mcp and then wrap the original npx command with codex sandbox --permission-profile memory-mcp to limit where the server can write and to prevent it from accessing the network:

TOML

Before starting the server, create its data directory and populate the npm cache with the pinned package. That lets npx --offline launch the server under a profile that disables network access:

Bash

Once the package is cached, Codex can start the memory server without network access, with writes limited to the npm cache and the server’s data directory.

Codex sandbox implementation

The sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

Network proxy

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

In the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI. When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

The network proxy is responsible for implementing the network restrictions defined in a permission profile. For example, the dev profile shown earlier allows requests to *.openai.com and explicitly denies requests to evil.example. When a request targets a domain that does not match an allow or deny rule, the proxy can suspend the request while it delegates to the harness for approval. Like the shell command example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review. Upon receiving a decision, the proxy either allows the request to proceed or rejects it with an error response.

The order matters here because even a DNS lookup can leak information encoded in a hostname. The proxy therefore resolves the requested hostname only after determining that it is allowed or approved. Note that broad wildcard rules or access to DNS services can still permit DNS-based exfiltration.

macOS

On macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt, Apple’s kernel-enforced sandboxing mechanism. Seatbelt policies are written in Sandbox Profile Language (SBPL), a Scheme-based language for expressing sandbox restrictions. Codex invokes Seatbelt through macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec command. Like codex sandbox, it takes options describing the sandbox followed by the command to run:

Bash

The PROFILE is a string of SBPL that contains entries that configure the sandbox. For example, the following SBPL snippet makes /dev/null and /dev/zero readable and writable under the sandbox policy:

Scheme

When the network proxy is enabled as part of a sandbox invocation, rules like the following are injected into the profile to limit connections to the appropriate local ports:

Scheme


Codex’s base profile starts with (deny default), so outbound connections remain blocked unless explicitly allowed.

Finally, the SBPL can contain placeholders using (param):

Scheme

which are populated by the -Dkey=value options passed to sandbox-exec.

To implement its own sandbox API, Codex builds up the list of arguments to sandbox-exec starting from a base policy, and then uses permission_profile and other context to amend it to produce the complete Seatbelt profile. The resulting profile and accompanying -D arguments configure the restrictions enforced by Seatbelt, while the network proxy enforces additional network rules. With the full arg list assembled, the invocation of sandbox-exec is straightforward.

Generating the correct SBPL is challenging because Apple does not document the language for third-party use. Indeed, man sandbox-exec states The sandbox-exec command is DEPRECATED (as is the sandbox_init() library function documented via man 3 sandbox_init). Despite the deprecation warning, macOS still ships Seatbelt profiles in /usr/share/sandbox, and third-party software, including Google Chrome and Chromium, continues to rely on Seatbelt. As such, we plan to continue to use Seatbelt for the foreseeable future.

Linux

To create the sandbox on Linux, Codex uses a combination of bubblewrap (bwrap), a command-line tool for constructing isolated environments, and seccomp-bpf, a Linux kernel mechanism for filtering system calls. An internal helper named codex-linux-sandbox coordinates the setup. Like sandbox-exec on macOS, it takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run:

Bash

When filesystem isolation or proxy routing is required, codex-linux-sandbox invokes bwrap to create the initial sandbox environment. bwrap then launches codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec inside it. This second invocation uses seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions before running the user’s command.

To construct that initial sandbox environment, Codex uses bubblewrap to create a filesystem view in a separate mount namespace that reflects the permission profile’s filesystem rules. Because this is fundamental to the sandbox implementation, Codex vendors its own copy of bwrap in case the user has not installed their own, but it prefers a compatible installation of bwrap found on PATH, when available. Empirically, some Linux distributions disable access to user namespaces by default, but grant an exception for the system bwrap.

Also like sandbox-exec, bwrap takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run within the sandbox. Instead of using a custom config language like SBPL, bwrap uses individual flags for configuration. Codex uses the following options to create the filesystem view:

  • --bind to specify a writable file or directory

  • --ro-bind to specify a read-only file or directory

  • --perms 000 --tmpfs DIR --remount-ro DIR to deny access to DIR

  • --perms 000 --ro-bind-data FD FILE to deny access to FILE (where FD is an open file descriptor to /dev/null)

To apply deny globs using these options, Codex expands them to concrete paths before launching each command. New matching paths are not automatically added to that command’s sandbox restrictions.

Codex also specifies options such as --unshare-ipc and --unshare-pid to prevent the sandbox from accessing other types of resources on the host, so bubblewrap affects more than just file visibility.

When using bubblewrap, Codex passes --unshare-net whenever networking is disabled or connections must go through the network proxy, which will create a new network namespace for the sandbox. We then use seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions on the networking system calls and socket families available to the command.


Specifically, we use the seccompiler crate to dynamically compile a BPF program based on the desired filters and apply it to a launcher process in the sandbox so the constraints are inherited by the entire process tree. As such, bwrap does not run the user’s command, but runs the codex-linux-sandbox launcher with its own config args followed by the user’s command:

Bash

To apply seccomp filters without elevated privileges, the launcher sets Linux’s no_new_privs flag. This flag is inherited by child processes and prevents them from gaining additional privileges when executing another program, such as a setuid executable.

The seccomp filters depend on the network configuration. When network access is disabled, we block a number of network-related syscalls, such as connect(2) and bind(2). Though when the network proxy is enabled in the sandbox, we allow IP sockets so the TCP listener created by codex-linux-sandbox can be reached, but block the creation of standalone Unix domain sockets by default, as those could enable inadvertent access to resources from the host.

Connecting to the network proxy

When the sandbox configuration merits the use of the network proxy, the Codex harness creates one instance of the proxy that can be reused across multiple invocations of codex-linux-sandbox within the same Codex thread. Each sandbox needs a way to reach that shared proxy from its isolated network namespace. Codex provides a loopback TCP listener inside that namespace and arranges for a process outside the sandbox to accept its connections and relay them to the proxy.

The following diagrams illustrate this setup for one proxy endpoint, with one connection through it shown in the final diagram. Before launching bubblewrap, codex-linux-sandbox creates a Unix socket pair to serve as a control channel and forks itself. The child runs run_host_bridge() and waits to receive the listener’s file descriptor over that channel:

In this example, the parent process uses exec to replace its program image with bwrap. This sets up the sandbox and launches codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec within it, passing along the FD for the control channel:

Inside the sandbox’s network namespace, the second invocation of codex-linux-sandbox creates a loopback TCP listener and passes its file descriptor via the socket. The listener remains associated with the sandbox’s network namespace, allowing the child process that remained outside the sandbox to accept connections from sandboxed programs while opening its upstream connections in the host’s network namespace. After the handoff, both processes close their control-channel descriptors, and the process inside the sandbox closes its copy of the listener.

Once the TCP listener is ready, the process inside the sandbox sets the appropriate value for HTTP_PROXY and related environment variables to point to that listener. It then applies seccomp before forking and executing the user’s command:

The process outside the sandbox keeps the listener open. For each accepted connection, it opens a connection to the configured proxy and relays data in both directions.

This additional machinery gives the command its own network namespace, including a separate loopback interface. On macOS, Seatbelt allows the command to connect directly to specified ports on the host’s loopback interface. On Linux, the command instead connects to a listener inside its isolated namespace, and a process outside the sandbox relays those connections to the configured proxy. The descriptor handoff makes this connection possible without exposing the host’s network namespace to the command.

Windows

Earlier this year, we implemented and wrote about our sandboxing efforts on Windows. Since then, Microsoft has released a library called MXC alongside new features for process isolation inside the Windows operating system. We are currently replacing our existing sandbox with one that makes use of the MXC library.

What is MXC?

MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container) is a sandboxed code execution system from Microsoft that supports several containment backends across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Codex supports an MXC-based sandbox on compatible Windows devices, using native process isolation to restrict commands within the user’s existing environment.

We are transitioning to MXC to improve security and usability while addressing several limitations of our existing Windows sandbox:

  • Need for elevated/admin access to set up the sandbox

  • Expensive/slow ACL checking and setting operations

  • Persistent sandbox setup state on the host machine, including

    • ACLs

    • Firewall rules

    • Sandbox users

    • Control plane files

MXC exposes a JSON configuration schema. Codex uses the MXC SDK to construct an execution request following that schema and containing the command, working directory, environment, and permissions. Those permissions cover filesystem and network access, along with Windows resources such as the desktop and clipboard.

Translating policy into MXC invocation

Codex uses fixed settings for several controls to balance compatibility and security. It permits registry reads and retains the Win32k and desktop access PowerShell needs during startup. Clipboard access, input injection, and desktop and system-settings controls are disabled. Finally, MXC is prevented from falling back to modifying host filesystem permissions.

Codex translates the permission profile’s filesystem and network rules into MXC’s configuration. Using the earlier dev profile, and assuming:

  • C:\, D:\ and Z:\ are the machine’s only local drives.

  • The workspace root and working directory are C:\work\demo.

  • The user’s home directory is D:\Users\dev, so ~/build-cache resolves to D:\Users\dev\build-cache.

  • The deny glob matches only C:\work\demo\config\dev.env and C:\work\demo\config\prod.env.

The corresponding MXC settings would include:

JSON

Drive-root access

MXC’s filesystem policy denies access by default. Codex therefore adds read-only grants for the local drive roots to provide the broad reads allowed by this profile. These grants apply recursively, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions.

One wrinkle: writable drive-root grants do not apply recursively, so Codex expands them to include the drive’s existing immediate children.

Conflicting grants

More-specific paths override ancestor grants, so C:\work\demo can be writable beneath a read-only C:\, while C:\work\demo\.git remains read-only.

When different path spellings or symlink/junction aliases refer to the same path, MXC applies the stricter permission: deny takes precedence over read-only, which takes precedence over read-write.

Deny globs

MXC takes concrete deny paths only, so Codex expands deny globs to matching files and directories before launch. New paths that match the glob are not automatically added while the command is running.

Network access

Domain rules such as *.openai.com are enforced by the shared Codex network proxy described earlier. Codex runs that proxy outside the sandbox and passes its addresses to the command through the same standard *_PROXY environment variables as mentioned previously. MXC blocks direct external connections while allowing host-loopback connections, including access to the proxy. Other local services remain reachable.

Across macOS, Linux, and Windows, the harness uses the same sandbox API to launch commands under a permission profile. The platform-specific implementations handle the setup needed to apply those restrictions.

Building on the Codex sandbox

Writing and executing code gives agents a flexible way to solve problems beyond software development. The Codex sandbox lets them use that capability in the user’s existing environment with explicit limits on filesystem and network access. It is a reusable primitive within the harness, and the codex sandbox command makes it available to tools you build yourself.

As agents take on more tasks, we want to make sandboxing practical for more tools and environments. That means making permissions easier to configure and taking advantage of better operating system protections as they become available. Our goal is to expand what agents can do while keeping people in control of what they can access.

item.title: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast
item.description: Learn how OpenAI built the Performance Factory, a system of Codex-powered workflows that finds and fixes performance issues to help keep ChatGPT fast.
item.content:encoded:
The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

The path from manual investigations to automated workflows

As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:

  • Find when the slowdown began

  • Identify the affected requests

  • Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it

We tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

The Performance Factory system’s four parts

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

Task service with configurable workflows

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

Plain text

A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

Each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

Dispatch loop that assigns work

A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

Codex in the cloud

Once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

The agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

Subscriptions that wake the agent when something changes

Some work has to wait for a person or a deployment; an agent shouldn’t have to keep running in the meantime. When a task needs to wait, it can subscribe to events like review comments or failed CI checks on a GitHub pull request to get notified when it’s time to pick the work back up. When an incoming event matches the subscription, the task becomes ready again and the dispatch loop can then assign an agent to continue the work.

The first workflow: from alert to recovery

Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation, root caused, fix proposed, and resolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

Agents find the root cause

Finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The perf-forensics skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

Once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

Adversarial review strengthens the diagnosis

Early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. If a rollout caused the slowdown, did similar requests that weren’t exposed stay healthy? If the suspected change was rolled back, did the affected metric recover?

In one investigation, an agent traced failing ChatGPT conversations to errors in image downloads and marked the cause as found. The Codex reviewer noticed that the internal service responsible for locating files had already recovered while image requests were still failing. The diagnosis did not explain the continuing failures, so the AI reviewer reopened the investigation and recorded what still needed to be established.

We’ve had success breaking larger jobs into focused Codex turns. In a manual review of 100 root cause suggestions, we graded 70% as accurate, with 30% needing further refinement or not fully establishing causality. In the Regression Workflow, different turns investigate regressions, challenge diagnoses, and propose fixes to increase accuracy numbers through checks and balances.

Fixing the regression is the hard part

Once the diagnosis passes adversarial review, the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request. An engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it. We’ve put a significant amount of work into making this handoff as easy as possible. Each task has a report with an automatically generated summary of the regression, its impact, the root cause, and the proposed fix. We’ve tuned these summaries to be easy to scan, including metrics time series, CPU flame graphs, and traces to help engineers quickly understand the findings and inspect the evidence. Engineers can edit the PR directly or use the diagnosis to write their own fix. If they leave comments on the PR, the workflow wakes an agent to address them.

After an engineer deploys the fix, the workflow wakes an agent to check whether performance has returned to its earlier baseline. If it has, the agent marks the task as resolved. If performance has only partially recovered, the agent resolves the original regression and opens a new task for the remaining slowdown, which may have a different cause. If there’s no improvement, the agent records what happened and sends the regression back for investigation.

Getting fixes right has been harder than finding the cause. For example, we’ve seen cases where the agent-proposed changes are more complicated than necessary or introduce new issues. Similar to the root cause step, we added an adversarial review of each proposed fix to check whether they address the root cause and help catch bugs or unintended consequences. Some fixes also require higher level architectural decisions. For example, adding a cache might improve performance but introduce stale data. Changes like these benefit from guidance from an engineer who knows the service and can weigh the tradeoffs.

We’re building an evaluation and improvement loop using these cases. By comparing the fixes agents propose with the changes engineers ultimately merge, we can better understand where proposals fall short, build evals, and improve the workflow. We’re also working on using synthetic performance tests so agents can measure proposed fixes and revise them before asking an engineer for review. We’re also exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop.

What we learned

Building and running the Performance Factory has taught us a lot about developing and operating agent workflows in production. Here are some lessons for teams building their own agentic workflows.

Protect engineers’ attention

The raw output from a Codex investigation can be a wall of text that’s hard to parse. It takes effort to figure out what the agent is claiming and track down the graphs to see whether the data backs it up. We want engineers to spend their attention on decisions rather than reconstructing the agent’s work.

Agents can investigate more regressions than a team has time to read about. Our first version gave engineers a UI full of findings, but someone still had to decide which information mattered. One regression can also appear as several incidents across alerts, monitors, and channels. The workflow now links related incidents, groups them by the metrics teams care about, and ranks their estimated impact. Engineers can focus on adding context, weighing tradeoffs, and deciding what to ship.

Evaluate changes to your agents

Updating an investigation skill or upgrading the model can make the agent better at diagnosing some cases and worse at others, so we need to test their impact before updating them. We test two things separately: 1) how well the agent investigates and 2) how useful its summaries are to engineers.

Evaluating investigations

For investigations, we backtest against past production incidents. We turn those incidents into a suite of test cases we can rerun when we change the skill. A Codex agent attempts to investigate and resolve the incident, and we compare the agent’s behavior to the actual past resolution data. Each case starts with a fresh Codex investigator and the original signal, stripped of details that might give away the answer.

Historical tests need care. Metrics and traces expire, while evidence collected after recovery can give away the cause. A test is only useful if we understand what evidence the investigator could see. The agent can inspect code and query production telemetry within set limits. It cannot use saved memories (notes from earlier investigations), read the incident writeup, or see results from previous runs. We also inspect its transcript afterward for information that might have spoiled the test.

We score when the problem began, how large it was, and which requests were affected. We also evaluate how the agent uses evidence to rank possible causes and explain what remains uncertain. An agent can get the timing right and still blame the wrong deployment, so we score those separately.

Evaluating agent-to-engineer handoffs

We evaluate task summaries using snapshots of saved tasks. These make particularly good backtests because summarization does not depend on external metrics or traces that expire. A separate grader checks whether an engineer unfamiliar with the system can understand what happened and why it matters, whether useful charts were kept, and whether the proposed next step is supported by the evidence.

Turn recurring failures into self-repair

Lastly, our agents need monitoring just as much as the services they investigate. A broken profiler or a missing permission can keep an agent from verifying what caused a slowdown. Those failures can be hard to spot in the final report, so we run an agent every day to look through messages and logs from recent runs for tool failures and access errors.

We use the Performance Factory to self-repair and fix the problems this check uncovers. When the same tool error blocks several investigations, the agent creates a task to fix it. If the cause is clear, an agent proposes a fix, and an engineer reviews the change and decides whether to merge it. After merging changes like this, we also use evals to check whether agents can get past the step that previously blocked them.

What’s next: broader applications, proactive monitoring

The Regression Workflow is just one instance of the agent factory pattern that moves tasks through explicit states. Agents advance the task when more work is ready; separate reviewers challenge the conclusions; engineers step in when the next decision requires judgment. Other workflows can reuse the same machinery with different states, instructions, and events.

Currently, our Regression Workflow starts when an alert fires. However, we’re working on more proactive ways for the Performance Factory to find slowdowns and optimizations even when no alert fires. We want agents to use the large amount of fine-grained performance data we already collect to spot regressions our alerts miss or discover optimizations. By comparing different kinds of data (batches of CPU and memory profiles, heap dumps, and request traces across releases), an agent might notice a small increase in CPU for a given request. It can then open a task in the Regression Workflow to trace the increase to its cause, implement a fix, and open a PR for an engineer to review.

In cases where we already know what to look for, we’re working to encode known signals into more Performance Factory workflows. Our service rightsizing skill, for example, helps agents spot autoscaling settings that keep more replicas running than a service needs. When we learn to recognize a pattern like that, we want to build and regularly run a workflow for it across all our services, constantly optimizing in a rapidly changing environment. With the Performance Factory, what an engineer learns from one slowdown can shape how we investigate and fix the next one, even months later in a different service.

Next time you’re using ChatGPT and notice a slowdown, there’s a good chance the Performance Factory is already figuring out why. Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We’re already exploring whether agents can do this themselves. As product development keeps accelerating with Codex, performance systems need to become increasingly autonomous and self-improving to keep up. Codex already helps us build ChatGPT faster. Now it’s helping us keep ChatGPT fast.

item.title: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI
item.description: A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.
item.content:encoded:
Company size: EnterpriseRegion: Asia-Pacific & OceaniaProducts: ChatGPT, CodexIndustry: Services

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

Gilbert + Tobin is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

Sam, what is Gilbert + Tobin trying to achieve with AI?

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

You describe Gilbert + Tobin’s journey in three phases: experimentation, personal productivity, and organisational productivity. How did the firm get started?

When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

Governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

You’ve noticed that adoption is unusually high for your firm, with 87% active usage among enabled ChatGPT users, more than twice the rate Gilbert + Tobin typically sees for other tools. How did leadership shape that culture?

Leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into new technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

You have made ChatGPT central to your own work. What have you learned from what you’ve built?

To help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins) using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

With a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s important to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

What advice would you give other CEOs beginning this journey?

Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

The opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.
